title: Recognition and the Kid Thomas trip to Russia
summary: He is grateful for recognition and describes jazz audiences and bands in Russia.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: How do you feel now, I mean, you know, like in the last few years, you've been getting a lot more recognition for your playing than you used to? You know, like, you know, one thing is, you know, like the Novak tape. I suppose going on tour with the Jaffees. I mean, how do you feel about, you know, just...

I feel very grateful and thankful for it, because what you're saying, as a subject, if it wasn't for that police officer enough, we wouldn't have had that opportunity to do that. The preservation people are doing it for us. Other guys, a higher class, like when they had the big band that was popular, they did it. Which I did in Chicago, I told you about that. But most of these guys didn't have that opportunity. And I am thankful for it. I was speaking for myself, for the President of the Hartwell, they did in the US, bringing us to these different places. I told you about the Fools we had in Russia.
No, I haven't heard that much about it. That was true.
Our government and the Russian government, I can tell you about that.

Yeah, I don't know how they selected this band. That's their business. Yeah. You see? And we were really treated very wonderfully. How was the response to... That's what I said, the response. They had three fans in there. They have a jazz, one city up in the government, and they have a jazz club, which I was very much surprised. In Russia? Because every place I went before that, they have them. Yeah. And I got some recordure they gave us. They copied the big bands back there when they were popular in the 30s, the farthest black and white, and they copied us everywhere I went, but I was surprised. And they had what we call a jam session. We do that, the manas jam, they mix that around. And they had, it looked like it was a small theater. They had three different bands I could see. But the proper one was six, some was seven, some was eight. And the trouble there with the banjos, it's hard for them to get good banjos. The only way they can get it closer is through East Berlin. So I told them, I said, in West Berlin, I know there's a bigger company kind of company, because Kim Warren, his band, he bought from there. It's a very good banjo. But the other instruments are pretty good, very good. And those guys can play. They can play, yeah.
And they play jazz in Russian?

I'm telling you, when I'm talking to some of you they're playing just like us. They're playing Sedition and some of them are playing Dixieland. And they have the all-in-folk songs. Like when you're in the hotel you stay and you go in the dining room where they have, you know, bands just like that. They use their folk songs and some of them switch around to, like I tell you, I did my time, but different types of music. You see? And they're very ordinary. Very ordinary. It's like it's supposed to be. I don't see anybody can cheat over there. I don't think. We want to revisit each city we were in. We'd be a week and we'd have one or two days. They'd be sponsored by the government for sightseeing. And besides that, Redmen and I, we'd go out ourselves and walk. We didn't know where we were. We'd use a guideline, you know, like the Indians do right there. And they're all friendly. They know you. They know where you were. They got the news from it. And they look at you and tell you you're not them. The Redmen almost looked like a Russian. A lot of people confused. They said, no.
They said, no, I'm from the state in New Orleans. And I said, no, no.

And with some place we stopped going to Russia, met a couple, men and his wife. Something like I'm talking to you. I like to talk to you if you want me to talk. Anyway, I got to talk to them and I found out that the wife was born in Russia. She speak of Russia. No, they're from St. Paul, Twin City. And they wanted to visit Russia. We were on the same plane and everything. And the plane stopped and everything. That's why I got to talk to them. And I met some Africans. I forgot what part of Africa. They were studying science, engineering, doctors and everything. But the Russian was studying. And the musicians, they were playing Dixieland and they were playing traditional music too. And we made a lot of friends. A lot of friends. And some of those places, I guess they sold a lot of tickets a lot of people wanted to go. That's why I was there a week in one place, you know, to give other people a chance to see. And when we would, the San Bernardino States, when you're in the band, a lot of time come here and it's leaving, where it's playing, everybody wants you to hurry up and sign, you know, and you ain't got time. You push the time. People would stand out there the bus in the cold, which wasn't cool for them because it was cool for us. I didn't see no sun on ice, but it was cool. They want to get to you. And I said, we have to get on the bus to get back, you see. And so what I'm subject to, the main part of the subject is that United States jazz is making history all over the world.
Yeah. And it's probably more appreciated in other places. That's what I'm talking about.
I didn't say it that way, but it's really appreciated.
